description: A chart-race comparison of how enterprises accelerated cloud spending—cloud leaders surged while on-prem and traditional managed hosting faced prolonged pressure. ⏱️ Timeline Comparison: How the Cloud Migration Stampede reshaped enterprise IT spending

In this video, we chart the race between cloud giants and the shrinking bucket of on-prem infrastructure and traditional managed hosting. Watch the “new gravity” pull budgets away from hardware-heavy spending—while AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accelerate through each migration wave.

📌 Chapters
00:00 — The setup: why cloud migration became inevitable
00:52 — 2015–2017: early lift, first big migrations
02:05 — 2018–2019: consolidation + container era boosts demand
03:15 — 2020: pandemic shift pushes spending online
04:12 — 2021: hybrid-to-cloud conversion turns into a stampede
05:30 — 2022–2023: cost optimization + AI pipeline buildout
06:55 — 2024–2025: cloud share keeps climbing despite macro pressure
08:10 — 2026 (estimated): where the chart race goes next

instagram_caption:
🚀 The Cloud Migration Stampede: watch budgets move in real time.

For years, “moving to the cloud” sounded like an IT project. Then it turned into a full budget rewrite. In this chart-race timeline, we compare enterprise infrastructure spending shifting from on-prem hardware and traditional managed hosting into the three dominant public cloud platforms: AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

Back in 2015, on-prem data center & infrastructure spending sat around **$195B**. Traditional managed hosting was also sizable at about **$85B**. Meanwhile, AWS infrastructure revenue was roughly **$25B**, Azure about **$10B**, and Google Cloud only **~$2.5B**—the giants were still “forming,” not dominating.

Then the momentum hit. In 2018, AWS climbed to **$56B** and Azure to **$24B**, while on-prem slipped to **~$183B**. By 2020, the shock of forced digital acceleration pushed cloud demand hard: AWS reached **~$80B**, Azure **~$41B**, Google Cloud **~$13B**, while on-prem drifted down to **~$170B** and managed hosting peaked around **~$92B**.

The real stampede came from 2021 onward. AWS rose to **~$90B** in 2021, then **$100B (2022)** and **$110B (2023)**—while on-prem kept bleeding, moving to **~$155B by 2023**. Azure’s trajectory was the standout pressure too: from **$60B in 2021** to **$70B (2022)** and **$82B (2023)**, with Google Cloud climbing from **$18B to $30B** across the same window.

By 2025, the split looks dramatic: AWS is at **$140B**, Azure at **$108B**, Google Cloud at **$42B**, while on-prem sits around **$146B** and managed hosting around **$82B**. The 2026 (estimated) projection pushes AWS to **$155B** and Azure to **$123B**, with on-prem sliding further toward **$142B**.

What do you think is the biggest reason migration accelerated—**security comfort**, **cost optimization**, or **AI workloads**? Drop your answer and follow for more chart-race timelines.
